title: Tournament of Lawyers: The Transformation of the Big Law Firm
author: Marc Galanter · Thomas Palay

dup.label: elastic tournament second transformation big law firm

sib.t: The Elastic Tournament: A Second Transformation of the Big Law Firm

dom.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: The original model treats partnership as the tournament prize, implying that promotion concludes associate competition. But the supplied record also reports a later revision that preserves core tournament insights while extending competition beyond partnership into differentiated partner and off-track roles.
qs: - *The tournament.* "[T]he firm holds a tournament in which all of the associates in a particular   'entering class' compete" (100), and "awards the prize of partnership to the top n percent of the   contestants" (100), judged on "their production of two goods: high quality legal work and their   own human capital" (100).

Galanter & Henderson 2008 (held), with Galanter as co-author, corroborate "some of the core theoretical insights" (the smooth upward trajectory of partnership ranks against cyclical associate hiring) while replacing the single tournament with an "elastic tournament" that extends past partnership into an equity core and a widening mantle of off-track lawyers and non-equity partners.

kp.k: Historical framework, not direct evidence of AI restructuring
kp.d: This record reconstructs Galanter and Palay's 1991 book through a publisher catalogue, later scholarship and quotations preserved in Wilkins and Gulati 1998; the book itself and its empirical appendices are unavailable in the record. Its relevance to AI is the record compiler's framing of the associate pyramid, not an AI claim by the book's authors. The publisher describes a study of one hundred leading American firms.
qs: The book itself is not on file.
Tournament of Lawyers* traces in detail the rise of one hundred of the nation's top firms in order to diagnose the health of the business of American law.
That two-step reception — canonical model, then inversion of its labor-market premises — is exactly the position the book occupies in this project's argument about AI and the associate pyramid.

kp.k: Partner expertise and junior labor underpin the pyramid
kp.d: The reconstructed model assumes two ranks, partners and associates. Partners contribute reputation, clients and know-how but have limited labor capacity; juniors contribute labor while developing human capital. The firm organizes an exchange between these complementary resources. The record attributes this explanation to Wilkins and Gulati's gloss of the book, rather than presenting it as directly captured book text.
qs: The firm has two and only two ranks, partners and associates (100-01).
Senior   lawyers hold surplus human capital (reputation, clients, know-how) but finite labor; juniors have   labor but little human capital.

kp.k: Partnership prospects provide deferred compensation and production incentives
kp.d: In the reconstructed tournament, associates within an entering class compete for partnership awarded to a fixed top percentage. Assessment concerns both high-quality legal work and associates' development of their own human capital. Partnership functions as deferred compensation, while the chance of obtaining it forms part of current compensation. These are theoretical mechanisms, supported here by quotations and page references transmitted through Wilkins and Gulati.

kp.k: Fixed promotion commitments address opportunism on both sides
kp.d: The record presents the predetermined promotion percentage as protecting both parties to the human-capital exchange: it discourages associates from inferior work, taking partners' clients or departing before investment is recouped, while constraining firms from accepting associates' work and withholding the promised promotion opportunity. This is the model's incentive argument, not a separately reported empirical finding.
qs: The ex ante fixed-percentage promotion promise solves a two-sided   opportunism problem
it stops associates from shirking (producing inferior work), grabbing   (stealing partners' clients) or leaving before the firm recoups its investment
taking the work and refusing the promotion

kp.k: Promotion and associate leverage generate exponential growth
kp.d: The reconstructed growth mechanism links fixed-share promotion to repeated associate hiring: each new partner cohort must itself be supported by new associates, producing exponential firm growth in the model. The book's closing inquiry asks whether this engine can continue; the publisher describes institutional undoing as a possibility, not an established outcome or dated forecast.
qs: requires promoting a fixed share of each class, each cohort of new partners must   in turn be leveraged with new associates — so the firm grows exponentially (99).
the very causes of the spiraling growth of the large law firm may lead to its undoing.

kp.k: Up-or-out is typical but theoretically unnecessary
kp.d: The record explicitly distinguishes the tournament mechanism from mandatory dismissal of unsuccessful associates. Although firing losers is described as typical practice, the authors' model does not require it. This qualification limits any reading that treats promotion competition and up-or-out as inseparable.
qs: Up-or-out — firing the tournament's losers — is the   typical practice (100) but not a necessary part of the model (225, 100-01).

kp.k: Information liberalization helped transform the large law firm
kp.d: The chapter reconstruction contrasts the stable, relationship-based firm circa 1960 with a changing information environment. As reported through Galanter and Henderson 2008, the book associates declining restraints on information about prices, salaries, profits, clients and services with Bates v. State Bar of Arizona (1977) and the emergence of a celebratory legal press.
qs: the stable, relationship-based big firm before the transformation the book sets out to explain.
the demise of restraints on information about prices, salaries, profits, clients and services, sparked by *Bates v. State Bar of Arizona* (1977) and the emergence of a new, celebratory legal press

kp.k: Later scholarship challenges the original tournament assumptions
kp.d: The record reports that Wilkins and Gulati 1998 formalize seven assumptions and argue that none accurately describes contemporary elite firms. Their critique concerns universal competition, equal chances, absence of sabotage, alignment of partner and firm interests, two career periods, promotion rewarding associate production, and transparent rules. This is a later critique, not Galanter and Palay's own conclusion.
qs: Wilkins & Gulati 1998 (held) systematise the model into seven assumptions — universal competition, equal chances, no sabotage problem, partner/firm interest identity, two career periods, promotion as reward for associate production, and transparent rules — and argue that none accurately describes contemporary elite firms.

kp.k: Elastic tournaments extend competition beyond initial partnership
kp.d: According to the record, Galanter and Henderson 2008 corroborate some original theoretical insights through the contrast between steadily rising partnership ranks and cyclical associate hiring. They nevertheless replace the single promotion tournament with an elastic tournament continuing beyond partnership, involving an equity core and growing numbers of off-track lawyers and non-equity partners. This later account revises the original two-rank staffing model.
qs: the smooth upward trajectory of partnership ranks against cyclical associate hiring
an "elastic tournament" that extends past partnership into an equity core and a widening mantle of off-track lawyers and non-equity partners.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: No concrete claim or prediction about AI changing legal services is presented.
pts.d: The document is a structured record of Galanter and Palay's 1991 book, rather than the book itself. It reconstructs a historical explanation of large-firm organisation and growth: partners exchange human capital for associates' labour, and a fixed-percentage promotion tournament generates further associate hiring and potentially exponential growth. These are not AI claims. The record's compiler connects the book's later reception to a project about AI and the associate pyramid, but that connection should not be attributed to Galanter and Palay as an AI prediction.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: No AI-specific evidence is offered; the historical account draws on a publisher description and later scholarly engagements.
pts.d: The publisher describes a study of one hundred leading American firms. The record identifies firm-size data, regression results and graphs as the book's empirical materials, but states that these are not on file. The tournament argument is reconstructed through Wilkins and Gulati (1998) and Galanter and Henderson (2008), with some quotations attributed to the book through those works. These materials support the record's account of the historical model, not a demonstrated effect of AI.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI adoption horizon or conditions for AI-driven change are specified.
pts.d: The historical account concerns the emergence and transformation of large American firms, including their circa-1960 organisation and post-1970 growth. The reconstructed growth mechanism depends on promoting a fixed share of associates and hiring additional associates to work with the resulting new partners. The publisher presents possible institutional undoing as a qualified prospect, without a date. Later scholarship from 1998 and 2008 challenges or revises the model; none of these timeframes is an AI forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The historical subjects are large American law firms, partners and associates; no AI-affected population is identified.
pts.d: In the reconstructed model, experienced partners contribute reputation, clients and know-how, while associates contribute labour and compete for partnership as deferred compensation. The later reception described in the record broadens the staffing account to equity partners, non-equity partners and off-track lawyers. The document does not claim that AI displaces or augments these roles, changes client costs, or affects access to justice.
